claims.text: Mg-containing lightweight complex concentrated alloys can exist as a single-phase solid solution.
The target alloy's initial as-cast state is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial state contains no significant intermetallic precipitates.
Non-equilibrium alloy processing can produce chemical short-range-order states distinct from equilibrium states.
In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, CSRO drives nucleation of fine intermetallic precipitates from the metastable solid solution.
Thermal aging above approximately 500 °C causes the proposed intermetallic precipitates to nucleate and grow.
Fine intermetallic precipitates initially stabilize a protective passivating interface.
Fine intermetallic precipitates pin diffusion pathways.
Initial fine-scale precipitation transiently improves corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Initial fine-scale precipitation transiently improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Continued thermal exposure increases diffusion and causes precipitate coarsening and elemental segregation.
Precipitate growth and coarsening deplete protective elements from the matrix.
Coarsening-induced depletion of protective elements reduces corrosion resistance.
Coarsening-induced depletion of protective elements reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Increasing aging time should produce an initial improvement followed by degradation in both corrosion and oxidation resistance.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment is a relevant chloride-rich regime for testing corrosion behavior.
Temperatures above approximately 500 °C constitute the relevant high-temperature oxidation boundary for the proposed transformation.
Precipitate coarsening should correlate measurably with the loss of corrosion and oxidation protection.
